notes: All values come from StarterKit/SPEC.md. Money is integer ten-thousandths of a cost unit (cost 3 = 30000). A value is a game-model value unless its medium lists a source for that field in fieldSources.

sources.title: NPS: Commemoration of the Pony Express
sources.section: The Pony Express, first two paragraphs
sources.claim: The Pony Express relayed mail 1,966 miles in 10 days, about 316 km per day across the route. The game uses authored courier speeds of 40 and 200 km/day; these are not universal historical measurements.

sources.title: Smithsonian Libraries: The Chappe Semaphore
sources.section: The Chappe Semaphore, opening paragraph and tower illustration
sources.claim: From 1792, Chappe semaphore towers relayed coded messages using visible mechanical arms. The game's 200 km/hour is a simplified model value, not a fixed historical service speed.

sources.title: ITU: From telegraph to telephone
sources.section: From telegraph to telephone, paragraphs on Wheatstone in 1839 and Morse in 1844
sources.claim: Commercial electric telegraphy carried coded messages over wires in the 19th century. The game simplifies propagation and omits operator coding and relay time.

sources.title: ITU: Telephone history
sources.section: ITU based in Switzerland, paragraphs on the 1876 telephone patent and long-distance speech
sources.claim: The telephone was patented in 1876 and enabled speech over wire connections. Its modeled propagation and costs are teaching assumptions.

sources.title: Cisco: Introduction to DWDM Technology
sources.section: Chapter 1, page 1-7, Table 1-1 and preceding text
sources.claim: One digital voice channel (DS0) carries 64 kbps.

sources.title: Cisco: Introduction to DWDM Technology
sources.section: Chapter 1, page 1-7, Table 1-1 and preceding text
sources.claim: A T1 (DS1) carries 1.544 Mbps: 24 channels of 64 kbps plus framing.

sources.title: Cisco: Introduction to DWDM Technology
sources.section: Chapter 1, page 1-7, Table 1-1 and preceding text
sources.claim: A T3 (DS3) carries 44.736 Mbps, equivalent to 28 T1s or 672 voice channels.

sources.title: Cisco: Introduction to DWDM Technology
sources.section: Chapter 1, page 1-7, Table 1-2 and preceding text
sources.claim: SONET OC-3, OC-12 and OC-48 run at 155.52 Mbps, 622.08 Mbps and 2,488.32 Mbps.

sources.title: Fiber Optic Association: Optical Fiber for OSP Installations
sources.section: Chromatic Dispersion, paragraph on effective refractive index
sources.claim: Glass fiber has an effective refractive index around 1.45 and carries light at roughly two-thirds of its vacuum speed. The game rounds propagation to 200,000 km/s.

sources.title: ESA: Geostationary orbit
sources.claim: Geostationary orbit is about 35,786 km above the equator. Doubling that altitude gives the game's idealized minimum up-and-down path of 71,572 km; slant paths, processing and terrestrial links are excluded.

sources.title: NIST: Meet the Constants
sources.section: c: the speed of light in vacuum
sources.claim: The exact vacuum speed of light is 299,792,458 m/s, or 299,792.458 km/s.

intro: You are the Messenger-General of a young civilization. You never build or move its settlements: they grow on their own, and your job is to keep their messages moving.
People first talked face to face, then learned to write. Speech carries live voice only as far as someone can hear; writing can travel, but only as fast as whoever carries it.
concept: Every link has a message class: alert < text < live voice < data. A medium can carry its own class and anything lower, so a written message can also carry an alert, but a beacon cannot carry a written message.
Every link has a reach: how far one link spans. There are no relay chains in this game; one link must cover the whole distance.
briefing.example: Worked example (not one of your rounds): a shepherd 4 km from the village must warn of wolves within 15 minutes. A signal drum carries an alert, reaches 5 km and is heard at once, so it works and costs 2. A smoke beacon also works but costs 3. A foot courier carries text, which covers an alert, but at 40 km/day it needs 2.4 hours.
briefing.note: Figures in this game are simplified game-model values, not historical measurements, unless a source is cited.

request.story: Raiders are approaching. The lookouts must warn Ashford within 1 hour, and the village has 12 months before raids become a regular threat.

hints: Work through the method in order. 1) Class: can the medium carry an alert? 2) Reach: does one link span 25 km? 3) Delivery time: distance ÷ speed, against the 1-hour deadline. 4) Capacity: does it carry the 1 circuit needed? 5) Build time and cost: is it ready within 12 months, and which feasible medium costs least?

Worked step, class and reach: every Level 1 medium can carry an alert, but the spoken word reaches only 0.1 km and the signal drum only 5 km, so neither spans 25 km. The smoke beacon, the foot courier and the horse relay go on to the delivery-time check.

settlements.name: Ashford

settlements.name: Brennan's Ford

request.story: Ashford's merchants must send written orders to Brennan's Ford, 200 km away, and each order must arrive within 24 hours. The grain trade starts in 12 months.

hints: Work through the method in order. 1) Class: a written order is text. 2) Reach: one link must span 200 km. 3) Delivery time: distance ÷ speed, against 24 hours. 4) Capacity: 1 circuit. 5) Build time and cost: ready within 12 months, then the cheapest.

Worked step, class and reach: the signal drum and smoke beacon carry only alerts, so they cannot carry a written order, and the spoken word reaches 0.1 km. That leaves the two couriers. Now divide 200 km by each courier's speed and compare with 24 hours.

intro: The age of wires has arrived. Messages can travel down copper and later glass, and you choose between the newest technology and what is already in the ground.
concept: Delivery time is distance ÷ speed. A fast medium is not an instant one: a semaphore message at 200 km/h still needs time to cross a long route, while a wire carries a signal at once.
A live conversation is one circuit. A link must carry at least the number of simultaneous circuits a request needs.

Building a link has two parts: the physical plant (copper, ducts, fiber) is slow to build; the technology on it is quick. Plant already in the ground costs nothing and takes no time. A higher-rate technology on the same plant costs more but takes no longer.
briefing.example: Worked example (not one of your rounds): a text message must cross 60 km within 15 minutes. The optical telegraph moves at 200 km/h, so it needs 18 minutes and is too slow; the electric telegraph arrives at once. And if copper is already in the ground, a T1 pays only for its equipment: 20 instead of 35, ready in 3 months instead of 39.
briefing.note: Figures in this game are simplified game-model values unless a source is cited. Standard rates such as 64 kbps per voice channel and the T1, T3 and SONET line rates are real values.

request.story: Ships leave Kingsport on the tide. Written sailing orders from Ashford must arrive within 30 minutes, and the new trade route opens in 40 months.

hints: Work through the method in order. 1) Class: sailing orders are text. 2) Reach: one link must span 150 km. 3) Delivery time: distance ÷ speed, against 30 minutes. 4) Capacity: 1 circuit. 5) Build time and cost: ready within 40 months, then the cheapest.

Worked step, delivery time: the optical telegraph covers 150 km at 200 km/h, so it needs 45 minutes against a 30-minute deadline. The electric telegraph, the telephone and the wired carriers arrive at once, so for them the build time against 40 months decides what is left.

request.story: The two cities' exchanges need 20 simultaneous live calls between them, each heard within 1 second. Copper telephone plant already runs along the route. Demand peaks in 60 months.

hints: Work through the method in order. 1) Class: live voice, or a higher class. 2) Reach: one link must span 300 km. 3) Delivery time: within 1 second. 4) Capacity: 20 circuits. 5) Build time and cost: ready within 60 months; copper already in the ground costs nothing.

Worked step, capacity: 20 simultaneous calls need 20 circuits. The telephone line carries 1 and the analog carrier 12, so both fail even though copper is already in the ground. Compare the costs of the media that carry 20 or more.

intro: Your civilization now asks for broadband for whole regions, not one link between two places. Each request describes a service area: how many people, over how many km², how far from the backbone, how fast each person needs to go, and whether they move around.
concept: Peak demand = population × per-user speed × 10%: about one in ten users is busy at once.

Each wireless generation trades coverage for capacity. A tower serves only so many km² and so many Mbps, so towers = the larger of area ÷ coverage and peak demand ÷ capacity. Every wireless tier needs flat terrain, and fixed wireless cannot serve people who move.

Satellites ignore distance on the ground but not the sky: a geostationary message always travels about 71,572 km up and down, about 239 ms, so it can never meet a tighter deadline. Low-orbit satellites are only about 1,100 km up and down. Satellites cannot serve more than 50 people per km².
Fiber costs per route km plus equipment per person. Fiber already in the ground costs nothing to reuse, and on a lit SONET route the equipment costs half: that is the SONET-to-Ethernet upgrade.
In this era you choose only among network technologies. Older media still appear in the table for comparison.
briefing.example: Worked example (not one of your rounds): a flat valley of 1,000 km² with 2,000 people needing 10 Mbps each has peak demand 2,000 × 10 × 10% = 2,000 Mbps. 4G needs the larger of 1,000 ÷ 600 → 2 towers and 2,000 ÷ 300 → 7 towers, so 7 towers at 15 each: 105. Fixed wireless needs 2 towers at 20 each: 40. LEO costs 100 + 0.2 × 2,000 = 500.
briefing.note: Figures in this game are simplified game-model values unless a source is cited. The geostationary altitude and the speed of light are real values.

settlements.name: Great Steppe
settlements.reason: Herding families spread across the flat steppe want video calls with the city.

request.story: 1,500 herders move with their animals across 40,000 km² of flat steppe, 400 km from Ashford's backbone. Each needs 5 Mbps while on the move, and live video calls need the signal to arrive within 150 ms. Service must start within 48 months.

hints: Work through the method in order. 1) Class: every network medium carries data. 2) Coverage: flat terrain, moving users, and at most 50 people per km² for satellites. 3) Delivery time: the 150 ms deadline (satellites use only their up-and-down path). 4) Capacity: 5 Mbps per user. 5) Build time and cost: ready within 48 months, then the cheapest.

Worked step, coverage and delivery time: the herders move, so fiber and fixed wireless are out. The geostationary path takes about 239 ms, more than 150 ms, so it is late. 2G gives each user only 0.2 Mbps. Compare the costs of 3G, 4G, 5G and the low-orbit satellite.

request.story: 200,000 people in 50 km² of Port Merrow each need 100 Mbps at home, 10 km from the backbone at Merrow Harbour. A SONET fiber route is already lit along the way. Demand arrives in 18 months; there is no delivery deadline for this request.

hints: Work through the method in order. 1) Class: data. 2) Coverage: fixed homes on flat ground; check the satellite density cap (200,000 ÷ 50 km²). 3) Delivery time: no deadline here. 4) Capacity: 100 Mbps per user. 5) Build time and cost: ready within 18 months; fiber already in the ground costs nothing.

Worked step, coverage and build time: Port Merrow has 4,000 people per km², far above the satellites' cap of 50. Every wireless tier needs new tower sites, which take 18 months plus 6 months of radio work: 24 months, more than 18. Now look at what the lit SONET fiber route already gives you.
